::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Previous research on emotion regulation (ER) has primarily focused on individual strategies and their association with well-being and psychopathology.
Recent frameworks emphasize a context-sensitive, goaldependent approach, defining ER flexibility as the ability to adaptively adjust ER strategies based on contextual demands and personal goals.
Despite growing evidence for its relevance, a concise self-report measure designed to capture trait-level, strategy-independent ER flexibility has been lacking.
To address this gap, we developed the Flexible Emotion Regulation Scale (FlexER-Scale) and validated it using data from four independent samples (N = 1,019).

Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) in an independent sample examined the scale's structure; criterion validity was assessed via correlations with the WHO-5 Well-Being Index and the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ).
The final 10-item FlexER-Scale demonstrated good psychometric properties, including satisfactory item discrimination and high internal consistency (α = .85).
EFA suggested a two-factor structure differentiating hedonic and contra-hedonic ER flexibility, which was supported by CFA.
The FlexER-Scale showed a significant positive correlation with psychological well-being, driven by the hedonic factor.
Small but significant correlations with habitual reappraisal and suppression use provided initial evidence for discriminant validity.

The FlexER-Scale is a promising tool for assessing ER flexibility, offering a concise alternative to existing measures by capturing adaptive regulatory variability without relying on predefined strategies.
Future research should examine its construct validity, longitudinal stability, and predictive validity.
Given that the validation was based on predominantly student samples from a German-speaking context, broader generalizability remains to be established.

• Introduces the FlexER-Scale, a 10-item measure of ER flexibility • Captures goal-directed up-and down-regulation of positive and negative emotions • Two-factor structure (hedonic/contra-hedonic ER flexibility) confirmed by CFA • FlexER scores positively relate to well-being and ER strategy use

text.text: Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) captures situational, moment-to-moment variability and context-dependent fluctuations in ER success, whereas self-report scales assess more stable, trait-like flexibility.
Several self-report instruments related to regulatory flexibility have been proposed.

For example, the Coping Flexibility Scale (Kato, 2012) assesses the ability to modify coping strategies when they are ineffective, whereas the Flexible Regulation of Emotional Expression (FREE) Scale (Burton & Bonanno, 2016; Gonzalez-Escamilla et al., 2022) measures the ability to enhance or suppress emotional expression depending on situational demands.

text.text: Although these measures capture important aspects of ER flexibility, they typically focus on coping processes, expressive regulation, or general perceptions of strategy use, rather than flexible, context-dependent adaptation to personal goals.
Moreover, available flexibility measures are often lengthy, strategy-specific, or restricted to experimental contexts, limiting their applicability in larger or clinical samples.
Thus, at the time of our study, no brief self-report scale existed that assessed trait-level ER flexibility across contexts without relying on predefined strategies.
To address this gap, we developed the Flexible Emotion Regulation Scale (FlexER-Scale) as a concise, context-sensitive measure of adaptive, goal-directed, trait-level emotion regulation flexibility.
Its development was guided by established theoretical frameworks on ER flexibility and goal-directed emotion regulation (Aldao et al., 2015; Aldao & Tull, 2015; Bonanno & Burton, 2013; Tamir, 2016).

text.text: Our objective was to create items that assess emotion regulation across different situational contexts, covering both negative and positive emotions and reflecting hedonic and contra-hedonic regulation goals (context sensitivity).
The scale also captures variability in strategy use (repertoire) and the ability to adaptively switch strategies when current ones prove ineffective (responsiveness to feedback).
The FlexER-Scale is designed to be strategy-independent in that it does not assess the frequency or effectiveness of any specific, predefined strategy.

text.text: This study introduces the Flexible Emotion Regulation Scale (FlexER-Scale), a brief self-report measure of goal-dependent emotion regulation flexibility.

Unlike previous measures that focus on specific regulation strategies, the FlexER-Scale assesses the adaptive, context-sensitive use of emotion regulation strategies to up-or down-regulate both positive and negative emotions.
Its development was guided by theoretical frameworks that emphasize regulatory flexibility as a key determinant of psychological adjustment (Aldao et al., 2015; Bonanno & Burton, 2013; Tamir, 2016).
text.formatted: Its development was guided by theoretical frameworks that emphasize regulatory flexibility as a key determinant of psychological adjustment <ref type="bibr">(Aldao et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Bonanno & Burton, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Tamir, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings demonstrate satisfactory to good item characteristics.

Item difficulty levels were acceptable, and most items closely aligned with the ideal difficulty range (however, there is some discussion on how to interpret item difficulty in (personality) trait measures; see Reise & Revicki, 2015).

text.text: Item discrimination values indicate that the FlexER-Scale effectively differentiates between individuals with varying levels of selfreported ER flexibility.
Our findings further provide evidence for the factor structure and reliability of the scale:
The parallel analysis indicated the distinctiveness of two latent constructs: a hedonic and a contra-hedonic ER flexibility factor.

Although this pattern may initially appear counterintuitive, it aligns with research on goal-directed emotion regulation, which suggests that individuals may sometimes regulate emotions in seemingly paradoxical ways to achieve higher-order goals (Tamir, 2016).
text.formatted: Although this pattern may initially appear counterintuitive, it aligns with research on goal-directed emotion regulation, which suggests that individuals may sometimes regulate emotions in seemingly paradoxical ways to achieve higher-order goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Tamir, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported the two-factor structure identified in the exploratory factor analysis (EFA), with all items loading significantly onto their respective factors and adequate overall model fit.
The two-factor model also showed a significantly better fit compared to a one-factor model.
Notably, the exploratory factor analysis did not separate the theoretically proposed facets of ER flexibility such as strategy repertoire or switching tendencies.

Instead, items referring to the availability and switching of strategies loaded on a common factor, suggesting a more general flexibility trait reflecting the perceived availability and adaptability of regulation strategies.
In contrast, the second factor was primarily defined by items reflecting contra-hedonic regulation, such as reducing positive emotions or intensifying negative emotions when this serves a goal.

This pattern is consistent with theoretical accounts of goal-directed emotion regulation and may indicate that the factor structure reflects differences in regulatory goals across emotional valence rather than differences in regulatory processes.

Criterion validity analyses indicated a positive association between FlexER scores and psychological well-being (WHO-5), consistent with prior findings linking emotion regulation flexibility to mental health and adaptive functioning (Bonanno & Burton, 2013; Southward et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Criterion validity analyses indicated a positive association between FlexER scores and psychological well-being (WHO-5), consistent with prior findings linking emotion regulation flexibility to mental health and adaptive functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Bonanno & Burton, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Southward et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, only the hedonic ER flexibility factor showed a significant moderate positive association with well-being, while the contra-hedonic factor showed no significant association.

This differential pattern is consistent with theoretical accounts suggesting that hedonic ER flexibility (which reflects the ability to regulate emotions in line with one's hedonic preferences) may more directly translate into subjective well-being.

In contrast, contra-hedonic ER flexibility captures the ability to regulate emotions in seemingly paradoxical ways to serve higher-order goals, a capacity that may be less consistently tied to hedonic well-being and may even involve short-term affective costs.
One could speculate that contra-hedonic ER is more closely related to social and professional success than to personal well-being.

The moderate effect size of the hedonic factor, alongside the near zero association for the contra-hedonic factor, further supports the utility of retaining both factors rather than collapsing them into a single score, and suggests that the two dimensions may have distinct implications for psychological health.
However, the correlational nature of our study limits causal interpretations.
Longitudinal and experimental designs are needed to clarify whether ER flexibility promotes well-being or vice versa.

The present study further sought to establish a first estimate of the criterion validity of the FlexER-Scale by examining its associations with the ERQ, a widely used measure of habitual strategy use.
Both FlexER factors exhibited small but significant positive correlations with the ERQ Reappraisal subscale, while only
Factor 2 (contra-hedonic ER flexibility) showed a small negative correlation with the ERQ Suppression subscale.
These findings are theoretically coherent and consistent with the conceptual distinction between the constructs assessed by the two instruments.

The FlexER-Scale was explicitly designed as a strategyindependent, context-sensitive measure of emotion regulation flexibilitya higher-order meta-skill reflecting the adaptive selection and adjustment of regulatory strategies in response to situational demands and personal goals.

Specifically, "strategy independence" refers to the absence of strategy-specificitythe scale does not privilege any particular regulatory approachrather than the absence of any reference to regulatory variability.

While some items implicitly reference strategy breadth or switching tendencies, this reflects an inherent feature of the construct itself rather than a conceptual inconsistency: flexibility, by definition, involves access to and the ability to shift between multiple regulatory approaches.

The FlexER-Scale is nonetheless conceptually distinct from instruments such as the Coping Flexibility Scale (Kato, 2012) or the FREE Scale (Burton & Bonanno, 2016), which assess either the ability to modify ineffective coping strategies or the enhancement and suppression of emotional expression, respectively; the FlexER-Scale, by contrast, focuses explicitly on goaldirected, context-sensitive regulation across both hedonic and contra-hedonic goals.

text.text: In contrast, the ERQ assesses the habitual frequency of two specific strategies-cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppressionwithout regard to contextual appropriateness.

Given this difference in conceptual level, small correlations between the FlexER-Scale and ERQ subscales are not only expected but also desirable, as they indicate that the FlexER-Scale captures a broader, strategy-neutral dimension of regulatory variability rather than simply reflecting the frequency of any single strategy.

The observed small correlation coefficients fall within the range typically reported in the literature for associations between strategy-specific and flexibility-based measures, as seen in prior work with self-report flexibility instruments such as the FREE Scale (Burton & Bonanno, 2016).
text.formatted: The observed small correlation coefficients fall within the range typically reported in the literature for associations between strategy-specific and flexibility-based measures, as seen in prior work with self-report flexibility instruments such as the FREE Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Burton & Bonanno, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The positive direction of the correlations with ERQ Reappraisal suggests that individuals higher in ER flexibility may be more likely to draw on reappraisal as one tool within a broader adaptive repertoire, though the modest effect sizes reinforce that flexibility is not reducible to reappraisal tendency alone.
Notably, only the contra-hedonic factor (Factor 2) showed a small negative correlation with ERQ Suppression.

This pattern is theoretically meaningful: contra-hedonic ER flexibility involves the willingness to engage with or tolerate aversive emotional states in service of higher-order goals, which may be inversely related to the habitual tendency to suppress emotional expression.
However, given the small magnitude of this association, it should be interpreted with caution and warrants further investigation.
Importantly, the generally low correlations between the FlexER-Scale and ERQ subscales provide evidence for the discriminant validity of the FlexER-Scale.

This supports the view that emotion regulation flexibility, as operationalized by the FlexER-Scale, constitutes a conceptually distinct construct that is only partially overlapping with habitual strategy.

Such findings are in line with theoretical models positing flexibility as a higher-order regulatory capacity, rather than a function of any single strategy use (Aldao et al., 2015; Bonanno & Burton, 2013; Sanchez-Lopez, 2021).
text.formatted: Such findings are in line with theoretical models positing flexibility as a higher-order regulatory capacity, rather than a function of any single strategy use <ref type="bibr">(Aldao et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Bonanno & Burton, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Sanchez-Lopez, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should further validate and refine the FlexER-Scale in several key areas.
First, the stability of the factor structure should be examined in different populations.

Further, its predictive validity should be examined across different psychological domains such as resilience, psychopathology, and adaptive coping, to clarify its relevance in clinical and non-clinical contexts.
Second, assessing test-retest reliability will help determine the temporal stability of flexible emotion regulation and whether the scale reflects a trait-like or state-dependent construct.

Third, cultural and contextual influences on the flexible use of emotion regulation strategies merit further investigation, as ER flexibility may manifest differently across cultures and may thus influence its generalizability and relation to well-being.
The present validation was based on German-speaking samples, with a large proportion of students and relatively young participants.
Accordingly, the generalizability of the findings to other age groups, cultural contexts, and clinical populations remains to be established.
Fourth, future studies could complement traditional factor-analytic approaches with network-analytic methods to further explore the latent structure and interrelations of FlexER items.
Integrating factor and network models may provide additional insights into the organization of emotion regulation flexibility (e.g., Song et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Integrating factor and network models may provide additional insights into the organization of emotion regulation flexibility (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Song et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Fifth, a further limitation concerns the reliance on self-report methodology.
The FlexER-Scale captures individuals' perceived tendency to regulate emotions flexibly rather than directly observed regulatory behavior.
Self-reports may be influenced by self-perception biases and therefore may not fully reflect moment-to-moment regulatory processes in real-world contexts.

Future research should therefore combine the FlexER-Scale with multimethod approaches, such as behavioral paradigms, or experience-sampling methods, to more comprehensively assess emotion regulation flexibility.
Sixth, future research may also examine how ER flexibility relates to broader individual difference variables and self-regulatory adaptability constructs.

For example, attachment orientations have been linked to systematic differences in emotion regulation and may influence how flexibly individuals regulate emotions across interpersonal contexts (e.g., Domic-Siede et al., 2026).
text.formatted: For example, attachment orientations have been linked to systematic differences in emotion regulation and may influence how flexibly individuals regulate emotions across interpersonal contexts (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Domic-Siede et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Investigating such associations may help to further situate the FlexER-Scale within a broader framework of personality and interpersonal functioning.
Finally, studies should examine the neural and physiological correlates of ER flexibility.

Identifying brain activity and physiological markers could deepen our understanding of the mechanisms underlying adaptive emotion regulation (cf. Diers et al., 2023; Gärtner et al., 2019 Gärtner et al., , 2023)).
text.formatted: Identifying brain activity and physiological markers could deepen our understanding of the mechanisms underlying adaptive emotion regulation (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Diers et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Gärtner et al., 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Gärtner et al., , 2023))</ref>.

text.text: Overall, the FlexER-Scale represents a novel and promising tool for capturing goal-directed flexibility in emotion regulation.
Further validation across cultures and languages is needed before its broader application can be established.
Addressing these future directions will enhance its ecological and cross-cultural applicability and strengthen its value for both research and clinical contexts in mental health and well-being.
